title: Maximise Sum of Chained Pairs
statement:
You are given `n` pairs of integers `(a_i, b_i)`. You build a sequence of **distinct** pairs (each pair may be used at most once, and the sequence must contain at least one pair):

- The first pair of the sequence can be **any** pair.
- Every following pair `j` that comes right after pair `i` must satisfy `a_j ≤ b_i`.

The value of a sequence is the sum of the `b` values of all the pairs in it. Print the maximum possible value.

Note that `a_i ≤ b_i` is not guaranteed, and the order in which the pairs appear in the input is unrelated to the order in which you may use them.

**Follow-up:** The original interviewer did not give constraints, and the expected solution was a bitmask DP, which is why `n` is small here. If `n` were large, what structure of the "can follow" relation could you exploit?
inputFormat:
The first line contains an integer `n`.
Each of the next `n` lines contains two integers `a_i` and `b_i`.
outputFormat: Print a single integer: the maximum sum of `b` values over all valid sequences.

examples.explanation: Start with (8, 3), then (1, 6) is allowed because 1 ≤ 3. The sum is 3 + 6 = 9. Starting with (9, 2) and continuing with (1, 6) gives only 8, and neither (9, 2) nor (8, 3) can follow (1, 6) because 9 > 6 and 8 > 6.
The order (1, 4), (3, 6), (5, 9), (8, 2) is valid: 3 ≤ 4, 5 ≤ 6 and 8 ≤ 9. It uses every pair, so the answer is 4 + 6 + 9 + 2 = 21.

hints: Trying all orders of the pairs takes O(n!) time. Many different orders share the same set of used pairs and the same last pair.
Define dp[mask][last] as the best sum of a valid sequence that uses exactly the pairs in `mask` and ends with pair `last`.
Start from dp[1 << i][i] = b_i. To extend, pick a pair j not in the mask with a_j ≤ b_last and update dp[mask | 1 << j][j]. The answer is the largest value in the whole table.
